card.thesis: Indexing tax amounts to a slower inflation gauge costs a low-wage family with children a larger share of income than it costs a comfortable couple.
card.overturns: "Tax inflation adjustments fully protect every household from paying more as prices rise."

claim: Since 2018 federal tax amounts are adjusted with the chained CPI (C-CPI-U) instead of the regular CPI-U. For the tax year 2026 amounts, the statutory 12-month averages (September-August) show CPI-U up 33.76% from the 2016 window to the 2025 window but C-CPI-U up only 30.31%: amounts indexed from before 2017 (the 10% and 12% bracket limits, the earned income credit) are 2.648% lower than CPI-U indexing would give, and the upper bracket thresholds (2017 base) 2.308% lower - about 0.29 point a year. The 2026 joint 12% bracket ends at $100,800 instead of about $103,469. With the 2026 standard deduction unchanged, a married couple pays about $13 more at $100,000 AGI, $280 more at $200,000 (0.14% of AGI) and $378 more at $300,000. The maximum earned income credit for three or more children is $8,231 instead of about $8,449: a family earning $25,000 on the credit plateau gets about $218 less, 0.87% of its earnings - roughly 6 times the share lost by the $200,000 couple. Tax year 2026. Sources: 26 U.S.C. 1(f), 1(j)(3), 32(j); IRS IR-2025-103; FRED CPIAUCNS and SUUR0000SA0 (BLS).

assumptions: Tax year 2026 amounts are set from the Sep 2024-Aug 2025 averages; the counterfactual applies the same statutory windows and bases to CPI-U (the pre-2018 method).

FRED carries the latest (final) C-CPI-U values; the law uses values as published when the August initial value came out, so official amounts can differ by a few dollars (the formula reproduces the official 2026 amounts to within about $100 after rounding).

Counterfactual changes only bracket limits (and the earned income credit maximum); the 2026 standard deduction ($32,200) and $50 rounding are left as they are, so the household figures are a lower bound.
Households: married filing jointly, all income ordinary, standard deduction. Earned income credit family: three or more children, earnings on the plateau of the credit under both methods.
limits: History, not a forecast: measures the gap accumulated through the 2025 window only; the gap in future years depends on inflation. No personal advice.

novelty.note: Said prospectively (2013-2017 policy pieces): chained indexing raises taxes over time and erodes the earned income credit, hitting low-income families earliest. Not found: the realized gap for tax year 2026 (2.65% / 2.31%), the dollar effects (about $218 less maximum credit vs $13-$378 more tax for couples) or the share-of-income comparison (0.87% vs 0.14%).
